accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE GCSE Mathematics subject content (2013) A18, solve quadratic equations algebraically, and Common Core HSA-REI.B.4.b, solve quadratic equations by inspection, taking square roots and completing the square. Every worked answer was verified by substitution, for example 3 × 4² − 12 = 36 and (7 − 2)² = 25, and irrational roots are kept exact as 1 ± √5 with decimals only as approximations.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the named slips: giving only the positive root (the + only tile is refused with (−4)² = 16), rooting before isolating as if √(3x² − 12) were √3·x − √12, halving instead of rooting (x = 24.5 for x² = 49), the sign of p in (x + 1)² (the vertex at +1 triggers a sign message), stopping at x² = 25, and claiming x² = −9 has solutions ±3.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsqroot draws y = (x − p)² with a draggable horizontal line y = k and a draggable vertex, marks the intersections as the solutions, and adds an equation-undo stack with four operation tiles. The existing x² and x³ lesson has no lab and flagsqr models area squares, not graphs; the shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners see the two intersections appear at ±√k as they move the line, find the touch point at k = 0 and the miss below zero, then watch (x − p)² = q shift the same picture sideways so the solutions become p ± √q. Working backwards from target crosses shows the vertex is the midpoint and q is the half-gap squared.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: x² = 25 has one solution, x² = −9 has x = −3, square-root first for 3x² − 12 = 36, and x = 5 or −5 for (x − 2)² = 25. Each is settled by the next task and echoed in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five challenge questions rotate answer order and each distractor is tagged (plus, half, sqrtfirst, noroot, noshift, sign, neg, order) with a message that names the slip and shows the right working, such as divide by 2 first: x² = 25, and ±10 is the root of 100.

readability.evidence: Learner audience gates pass: kid paragraphs use short sentences and one step at a time with worked numbers like 3x² − 12 = 36; adult paragraphs keep the terms quadratic equation, root, isolate, ± and completed-square form while staying under the FK 9.5 target.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and low overlap with other lessons. Each paragraph gives a method, a graph link or a named mistake, and every practice and mastery explanation shows the working rather than restating the answer.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop: every Show me finishes inside the limit, the line and vertex have wide drag zones, four step buttons twin every drag, and operation tiles on the canvas are full-width finger targets on narrow screens.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas aria-label is updated with each readout including the current equation and its solutions, every drag and tile has a labelled button, theme colours are contrast-checked in both modes, and timers respect reduced motion.

sources: DfE (2013) Mathematics GCSE subject content and assessment objectives, A18
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (2010) HSA-REI.B.4.b
NCETM (2018) Secondary mastery materials: quadratic equations
